metaTitle: Salik Tolls in Dubai: What Every Visitor Needs to Know
metaDescription: Salik is Dubai's automatic road toll: AED 6 at peak, AED 4 off-peak, ten gates on the main roads. Who pays, where the gates are and how visitors avoid fines.
excerpt: Salik is Dubai's barrier-free road toll, charged per gate at AED 6 in peak hours and AED 4 the rest of the day. Visitors in a hired car pay through the rental company, taxis pay the same toll, and a chauffeur booking is fixed at the moment you book. Here is where the ten gates are and what goes wrong.
quickAnswer: Salik is Dubai's automatic road toll: a windscreen tag is read at ten gantries on Sheikh Zayed Road, Al Khail Road and the Creek crossings, and the charge is AED 6 per crossing at peak, AED 4 off-peak and free from 1am to 6am. You only handle it yourself in a hired car. Taxis pay the same toll, and with a chauffeur the price is fixed at booking.
content:
Salik is Dubai's electronic road toll, and as a visitor you never stop at a booth or hand over cash: a tag on the windscreen is read as the car passes under a gantry and the charge comes off a prepaid account. The rate is AED 6 or AED 4 per crossing depending on the time of day, and there are ten gates across the city. Whether it lands on you depends on how you get around: a hired car means you deal with it, a chauffeur means you do not.

What is Salik and how does it work?

Salik is a fully automatic toll with no barriers, no lanes to pick and no slowing down. The Dubai government portal explains that every vehicle carries a rechargeable Salik tag on the windscreen, and the toll is deducted from that tag each time the car passes through a gate.

The system is run by Salik on behalf of the Roads and Transport Authority (RTA). Its own operational review confirms that gates use plate recognition and RFID tags to charge the linked account automatically, with no ticket and no stop.

Salik at a glance

FactDetailSource
Peak rateAED 6 per crossing, Monday to Saturday, 6am to 10am and 4pm to 8pmDubai government portal
Off-peak rateAED 4 per crossingDubai government portal
Free window1am to 6am every dayDubai government portal
SundaysFlat AED 4 outside the free windowDubai government portal
Number of gatesTen, since 24 November 2024Salik operational review
Roads coveredSheikh Zayed Road, Al Khail Road, the Creek crossings and the airport tunnelSalik, How Salik Works
No tag or no balanceFines apply; an empty account must be topped up within 5 daysDubai government portal

How much does Salik cost per crossing?

AED 6 in peak hours and AED 4 the rest of the day, with nothing charged between 1am and 6am. Dubai charges by time of day rather than a flat rate, and the government portal sets out the current bands: peak is Monday to Saturday, 6am to 10am and 4pm to 8pm, at AED 6, everything else at AED 4.

Sundays are simpler. The same page states that a flat AED 4 applies all day on Sundays, excluding the free early morning hours.

Two things visitors miss. The charge is per gate, not per drive, so a run down Sheikh Zayed Road at 5pm can pass three or four gantries and cost AED 6 at each one. And the peak windows sit exactly where airport runs and hotel check-ins tend to fall, so the higher rate is the one you will meet most often.

Where are the Salik gates in Dubai?

There are ten gates, and nearly all of them sit on the two roads visitors use most. Salik's own map lists them as Al Mamzar North, Al Mamzar South, Airport Tunnel, Al Maktoum, Al Garhoud, Business Bay Crossing, Al Safa, Al Safa South, Al Barsha and Jebel Ali, strung along Sheikh Zayed Road and Al Khail Road.

The two newest gates opened on 24 November 2024. The RTA's announcement places Al Safa South on Sheikh Zayed Road between Al Meydan and Umm Al Sheif Streets, and Salik's review puts Business Bay Crossing on Al Khail Road.

There is one helpful exception. Pass both the Al Safa and Al Safa South gates in the same direction within an hour and you are charged once, not twice, which matters because the two sit only a short stretch apart.

Which gates sit on the common visitor routes?

  • Dubai International (DXB) into Deira or Bur Dubai: the Airport Tunnel gate sits on the airport approach, and Al Garhoud or Al Maktoum apply if you cross the Creek by bridge.
  • DXB to Downtown, the Marina or the Palm: expect the Sheikh Zayed Road gates in sequence, Al Safa, Al Safa South and Al Barsha, depending on where you leave the highway.
  • Dubai to Abu Dhabi: the Jebel Ali gate is the last one before you leave the emirate on Sheikh Zayed Road.
  • Dubai to Sharjah: the Al Mamzar North and South gates sit on the Sharjah side of the city.
  • Al Khail Road as a bypass: Business Bay Crossing is on that road, so avoiding Sheikh Zayed Road no longer avoids every toll.

Routing decides the bill more than distance does. Two hotels a few minutes apart can sit either side of a gate, and a driver who knows the side roads can pass under fewer gantries than a navigation app that always picks the highway.

Do visitors need a Salik tag?

Only if you are driving a car yourself. The tag belongs to the vehicle, not the person, and the government portal says tags are available online or at petrol stations, but visitors almost never buy one because a hired car already carries one.

If you hire a car, the rental company's tag is on the windscreen and the company tracks what you owe. How they recover it varies by company, so read the rental agreement before you sign and ask whether tolls are billed per crossing, with an admin fee, or settled from your deposit.

If you take a taxi, the toll applies to the vehicle in the same way. The portal is explicit that all vehicles, including taxis, are subject to the toll, so a metered cab crossing a gate is not exempt.

If you book a chauffeur, there is nothing to think about. An Emirates Limo chauffeur service in Dubai is priced at the moment you book, and that fixed figure does not change because the driver crossed a gantry, hit traffic or waited for a late flight.

What to have ready before you drive in Dubai

  • The rental agreement, with the toll clause read and understood
  • A note of the peak windows: 6am to 10am and 4pm to 8pm, Monday to Saturday
  • The gate list above, so you can count crossings on a planned route
  • A card on file with the rental company for toll settlement
  • A screenshot of the route you plan to take, to check against the final toll statement

How do the options compare for a visitor?

The table below is about who handles the toll and where the surprise comes from, not about price. Every option crosses the same gates; the difference is whether you find out about it before or after the drive.

How you travelWho deals with SalikWhere the surprise appears
Hired car, self-driveYou, through the rental company's tagOn the final invoice or deposit, sometimes weeks later, often with an admin fee
TaxiThe taxi operator, under its own policyOnly if the operator passes it on, which you find out at the end, so ask before you set off
Private chauffeurThe chauffeur companyNowhere: the price is fixed at booking and paid online before you travel

For a single airport run, the chauffeur option removes the most uncertainty. A private pickup at DXB or DWC is met in arrivals with a name board, the flight is tracked, and 60 minutes of waiting is included from the actual landing time.

What goes wrong with Salik for visitors?

The most common problem is a fine that arrives long after you flew home. The government portal warns that passing a gate without a tag can attract a fine, and so can passing with an empty account that is not topped up within 5 days. In a hired car that fine reaches the rental company first, and it reaches you with their handling charge attached.

The second problem is route choice. Drivers new to the city follow the highway by default, which on Sheikh Zayed Road means every gate in sequence, when a parallel road might cross one or none.

The third is timing. A 9am hotel check-out and a 5pm airport run both fall inside the AED 6 peak window, and a family in two hired cars pays every crossing twice.

Then there are the ordinary transfer failures that have nothing to do with tolls but hurt more when you are also watching a meter: a wrong terminal at DXB, a pickup that expires while you queue at immigration, or a late change of hotel that a taxi cannot re-price in advance. A pre-booked chauffeur solves those with flight tracking, a chauffeur waiting in the hall, and free cancellation up to 24 hours before pickup; the details are on the Emirates Limo FAQ.

Is it worth avoiding Salik gates on purpose?

Rarely. At AED 4 to AED 6 a crossing, a detour that adds 20 minutes on a hot afternoon costs you more in time than it saves in tolls. Where avoiding a gate makes sense is a short hop that just happens to sit across one, and a local driver already knows which those are.

If you are planning a full day of stops rather than one drive, book the car by the hour instead of counting crossings. An hourly chauffeur in Dubai starts from AED 150 per hour, the driver and car stay with you for unlimited stops, and the total is fixed when you book rather than assembled gate by gate.

Heading to Abu Dhabi for the day? The Jebel Ali gate is the only Salik crossing on the way out, and Abu Dhabi runs its own separate toll system, so a private Dubai to Abu Dhabi transfer with a fixed price is the cleanest way to cover both.

faqs.question: How much is the Salik toll in Dubai?
faqs.answer: AED 6 per crossing in peak hours, which are Monday to Saturday from 6am to 10am and 4pm to 8pm, and AED 4 per crossing at other times. Nothing is charged between 1am and 6am, and Sundays are a flat AED 4 outside that free window.

faqs.question: Do tourists have to pay Salik in Dubai?
faqs.answer: Yes, if they are in a vehicle that crosses a gate. In a hired car the rental company's tag records each crossing and bills you under the rental agreement, and taxis are subject to the same toll. With a pre-booked chauffeur the price is fixed when you book, so there is nothing to settle afterwards.

faqs.question: How many Salik gates are there in Dubai?
faqs.answer: Ten. They are Al Mamzar North, Al Mamzar South, Airport Tunnel, Al Maktoum, Al Garhoud, Business Bay Crossing, Al Safa, Al Safa South, Al Barsha and Jebel Ali. The last two, Business Bay Crossing and Al Safa South, opened on 24 November 2024.

faqs.question: Are Salik tolls charged twice at Al Safa?
faqs.answer: No. A vehicle passing both the Al Safa and Al Safa South gates in the same direction within one hour is charged a single toll. The two gates sit close together on Sheikh Zayed Road, so most drives through that stretch pay once.

faqs.question: What happens if a car has no Salik tag or no balance?
faqs.answer: A fine can be issued. The Dubai government portal warns that passing a gate without a tag may attract a fine, and that a vehicle passing with insufficient balance that is not topped up within 5 days is fined too. In a hired car the fine goes to the rental company, which passes it on with its own charge.
